title: A subcontractor's accommodation account and control of pay
narrative:
This is an authored intake file about a fictional construction project.

A union intake officer receives records from an adult worker engaged by a subcontractor on a building renovation. The principal contractor runs the site, while the subcontractor issues payslips. A separate accommodation business supplies beds and transport. The worker does not know whether the accommodation manager and subcontractor share ownership. Their names appear together on a leaflet, which supports asking about their relationship but establishes no particular financial arrangement.

Three bank deposits match the net amounts on the payslips. Each is followed by a transfer headed accommodation. The worker has supplied the amounts but has not authorized access to the bank account itself. A colleague concluded that matching deposits settle the wage question. The intake officer instead wants to establish who could use the money and whether each later transfer was a genuine choice. The latest account of card access appears in the records below.

The accommodation invoice includes bedding and a security deposit. A receipt shows that some bedding was purchased; it does not identify which resident used it or explain the amount charged to this worker. The worker disputes being responsible for a damaged locker and has asked for photographs. Neither side has supplied them. A signed induction form confirms that a room was allocated, but the form does not list repayment terms or authorize bank access.

There is a separate dispute about outdoor breaks during hot weather. A supervisor says work paused twice; the worker remembers being expected to remain beside the equipment. The supplied time sheet records paid hours without break details. That issue deserves checking on its own facts rather than serving as proof of every other concern.

The worker has asked about moving to another subcontractor on the same project. They would prefer to preserve the current room for a week while arranging alternatives. A relative suggests publishing the payslips online. The worker has declined because the records could identify the work team and because the housing charge may contain both valid and disputed items. The intake appointment is private; nobody has permission to confront the supervisor.

[CO-R1] Worker account: "The accommodation manager keeps my bank card and approval phone. I asked to make the transfers myself and was refused. I am told what part of each wage deposit I may keep."

[CO-R2] Supplied assignment reply: "You must remain on this assignment until the accommodation balance is paid. If you change subcontractors, we will keep your unpaid wages."

[CO-R3] Contact note: "I can meet the adviser outside work and use a separate private phone. Please ask before contacting anyone for me."
user_question: As the union intake officer, how would you explain the difference between the bank deposits, the worker's control of that money and the disputed accommodation balance? Identify proportionate first steps and the facts needed before approaching another organization. Preserve the worker's wish to stay employed if a safe, voluntary arrangement is possible.
